sections.title: Why big files don't belong in your database or app servers

blocks.text: Images, videos, documents and backups are large, immutable blobs. Storing them in a relational database bloats backups and the buffer pool; streaming them through app servers wastes CPU, memory and bandwidth. Object storage (S3, GCS, Azure Blob) is built for this: effectively unlimited capacity, 11 nines of durability, HTTP access, cheap tiers — and it pairs naturally with a CDN.

head: Store
What goes there
rows: Metadata: owner, key, size, content type, status, dimensions
Cached copies served close to users

blocks.caption: The app server never touches the bytes

items: Presigned URLs embed a signature for one operation on one key with an expiry — no credentials on the client.
Large files use **multipart upload**: parts of 5–100 MB uploaded in parallel and retried independently, then completed.
Validate after upload (type sniffing, virus scan, size) before marking the object usable.
Images: generate fixed sizes on upload, or resize on the fly at the edge with caching.
Video: transcode into multiple bitrates and segment into HLS/DASH chunks for adaptive streaming.
Idempotent workers keyed by object key + variant, because events can be delivered twice.
Public assets: CDN in front of the bucket, long TTLs, content-hashed keys.
Private assets: short-lived signed URLs or signed cookies (CloudFront), checked at the edge.
Range requests for video seeking and resumable downloads.
Never make the bucket itself public unless every object is meant to be.

cols.title: Erasure coding (e.g. 6 data + 3 parity)
pros: Survives losing any 3 of 9 fragments at ~1.5× storage
cons: CPU to encode/decode; reads touch several nodes

blocks.text: Large systems typically erasure-code across availability zones, keep metadata in a strongly consistent, sharded index, and continuously scrub data to detect and repair bit rot.

blocks.title: Say it in the interview
blocks.text: Clients upload directly to object storage with presigned multipart URLs; an upload event triggers idempotent workers that create variants; metadata lives in the DB; everything is served through a CDN with signed URLs for private content.
